clue.text: Fantastic gal saves city abroad

indicators.note: fantastic in the sense of wild or fanciful, so the letters of gal saves are freely rearranged

explanation.surface: A wonderful woman rescues some foreign city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nevada gambling resort is a city in the United States, so abroad from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: Hatred upset old prison guards of little depth

indicators.note: the reversed prison holds the next piece inside it, as guards surround a prisoner
in a down clue, upset means the word is turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: gaol is the old-fashioned British spelling of jail
something of little depth is thin, shallow

explanation.surface: Someone loathes an old jail whose guards are shallow people.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upset' turns the word upside down; 'old prison' is the old British spelling of jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name intense dislike or detestation; a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Way home blocked by van in accident black spot?

indicators.note: the way-and-home pair has the next letter stuck in the middle of it, blocking it

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
being in means being at home

indicators.note: the van is the front, so the van in accident is its first letter

explanation.surface: A road home is blocked by a van after a crash at an accident black spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'van in accident' looks like a lorry at the scene; van here means vanguard, the front, giving A.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark or blemish is a spot, often black or dark; the question mark flags the playful reading of the road-safety phrase.

clue.text: Thrill old flame gets greeting judge outside city

indicators.note: the judge piece stands outside the city, i.e. placed after it at the end

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, an old flame
hi is a casual greeting
LA is Los Angeles
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: A former lover's hello thrills a judge waiting outside a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to excite or elate someone greatly; a direct synonym.

clue.text: Illegal stuff guest and stoned hosts lost

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take in the next piece, as hosts take in a guest
stoned as in intoxicated, so the letters of guest and are scrambled

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for lost, as in sports results tables

explanation.surface: A guest and some stoned party hosts have lost their way on illicit drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stoned' rearranges GUESTAND into ANGEDUST, and 'hosts' puts L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Street name for the drug PCP (phencyclidine), an illegal substance, so illegal stuff.

clue.text: Companion following endless amphetamine talk

indicators.note: the companion piece comes after the shortened drug word
the slang word for the drug loses its final letter, so it has no end

parts.note: speed is street slang for amphetamine
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A friend comes after an amphetamine binge, still talking.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech is a formal talk given to an audience, so the noun senses match.

clue.text: Via the mouth, excite climax

indicators.note: something said by mouth is spoken, so the word is pronounced rather than spelt

parts.note: to pique curiosity or interest is to excite it

explanation.surface: An oral way to arouse someone and reach a climax.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak is the high point or culmination of something, the same as its climax.

clue.text: Run a piece about one devoted to Tuck?

indicators.note: about in the sense of around or turned round, so the letters of Run a piece are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to run a newspaper item about someone who loves Friar Tuck.
explanation.walkthrough: Tuck looks like Robin Hood's friar; here it is British slang for food, as in a school tuck shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A gourmet devoted to fine eating and drinking; tuck is British slang for food, so a lover of tuck fits.

clue.text: One pursuing strong desire to make good time

indicators.note: the good letter is swapped out to make way for the time letter in its place

parts.note: a hunger for something is a strong desire for it

explanation.surface: Someone in pursuit, with a strong wish to make good time.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who chases game or quarry is a pursuer; the noun is the agent of the chase.

clue.text: Lot using spades instead of last two clubs

indicators.note: using means the spades letter is brought in to be used
it takes the place of the final pair of letters of the lot word

parts.note: a batch is a lot, a group of items made together
S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A card-player's lot, playing spades in place of the last two clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-game picture makes 'clubs' look like a suit, but it is the definition: bats used in cricket or baseball.
explanation.definitionFit: A bat is a club used to hit a ball, as in baseball or cricket, so plural bats are clubs.

clue.text: Embarrass the latest member of Tea Party

indicators.note: the latest member is the one at the end, so the final letter of Tea

parts.note: a bash is an informal party

explanation.surface: A new recruit to the US Tea Party movement is made to feel embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tea Party is a US conservative political movement; 'member' suggests a person, but it is only the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash someone is to make them feel ashamed or disconcerted; a synonym.

clue.text: A fine transition (groin a tad irritated)

indicators.note: irritated as in inflamed or disturbed, so the letters of groin a tad are rearranged

explanation.surface: A delicate shift in feeling as someone's groin becomes slightly sore.
explanation.definitionFit: A gradation is a slight step in a gradual series, a fine transition from one shade or level to the next.

clue.text: Shall need to change section without a title?

indicators.note: the letters must change, being rearranged into a new order

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for section, as in legal documents

explanation.surface: A query about whether a section of a document must be altered if it has no heading.
explanation.walkthrough: A handle is informal for a title or name, so 'without a title' fits; the question mark flags that slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Handle is slang for a name or title, so lacking a handle means lacking a title, though literally it describes a cup or door.

clue.text: A noble expected to welcome knight

indicators.note: the expected word takes the knight in, welcoming him inside

parts.note: something due is expected, as a train due at noon
K is the chess notation for king, and also an abbreviation for knight in honours

explanation.surface: A nobleman is expected to receive a knight as his guest.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest rank of British peerage, so a duke is a nobleman of the top order.

clue.text: Police arresting married circus worker

indicators.note: to police is to control and put in order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Police are detaining a married man who works at the circus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police' looks like the subject of the sentence but is the anagram signal: ARRESTING plus M rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringmaster presents the acts in the circus ring, a circus employee.

clue.text: All Time Low managed tours 1D rejected

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the whole assembly is read backwards
the managed word goes round the next piece as a band tours a country

parts.note: to run something is to manage it, past tense ran
1D read as letters is I and D, the figure one standing for I

explanation.surface: The rock band All Time Low managed tours that One Direction turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: All Time Low and One Direction (1D) are pop bands; 'rejected' reverses RIDAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, so an all-time low.

clue.text: Happy area: road close to various boozers

parts.note: happy is a jokey euphemism for slightly drunk

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so the last letter of various

explanation.surface: A cheerful neighbourhood: the road close to various pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boozers' could be British slang for pubs, but here it means heavy drinkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy drinkers, people who booze habitually; the agent sense of boozers, not the British slang for pubs.

clue.text: Inappropriate, like a naked astronaut in space?

definitions.meaning: not suitable or fitting for a purpose

definitions.text: like a naked astronaut in space?
definitions.meaning: an astronaut with no spacesuit on is literally without a suit

explanation.surface: It would be unwise, and indecent, for a space traveller to float about bare.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfit or ill-matched for something; the second sense reads the word literally as lacking a spacesuit.

clue.text: Having loaded gun, very quiet editor and I intervened

indicators.note: the gun is loaded with the next pieces, which go inside it

parts.note: the Sten is a British submachine gun
PP is pianissimo, the musical marking for very quiet

explanation.surface: With a gun loaded, a hushed editor and the speaker stepped into a dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: To step in is to intervene in a situation; the phrasal verb is in the past tense to match.

clue.text: Lions playing in Africa? Hawks around Manx hill?

indicators.note: the selling word goes around the next piece

parts.note: to hawk goods is to tout them, and touts are sellers

indicators.note: a Manx cat has no tail, so the hill word loses its last letter

parts.note: a rise is a small hill or slope

explanation.surface: Questions about lions at play in Africa and hawks circling a hill on the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The British and Irish Lions are a rugby team that tours abroad, e.g. South Africa; Manx means from the Isle of Man, and Manx cats are tailless.
explanation.definitionFit: Lions rugby players visiting another country are on tour, so they are travellers abroad; the question mark marks the cryptic example.

clue.text: Something below heading for The Nautilus?

parts.note: the Nautilus is Captain Nemo's submarine in Jules Verne, so a sub
a title is a heading

explanation.surface: A query about what lies beneath the heading of Jules Verne's submarine.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and wordplay share the idea of a heading; the question mark flags the Nautilus as an example of a sub.
explanation.definitionFit: A secondary title printed beneath the main one sits below it, so something below.

clue.text: Muppet flipping vacuous Zambian slimed!

indicators.note: the exclamation marks the setter's liberty: slimed, read as goo'd, means goo is put round the rest

parts.note: slime is goo; the setter reads the word as goo'd, the slime word with -d

indicators.note: flipping means turned over, so the letters are read in reverse
vacuous means empty, so only the outer letters of Zambian remain

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry: a Muppet has gone and slimed some empty-headed Zambian!
explanation.walkthrough: The setter explained that 'slimed' is slime (goo) with -ed, i.e. 'goo'd', covered round with goo.
explanation.definitionFit: Gonzo is the hook-nosed stuntman puppet in Jim Henson's Muppet Show, so a Muppet by example.

clue.text: A professional cook

definitions.meaning: a qualified practitioner such as a physician
to cook the books is to falsify or tamper with them

explanation.definitionFit: A physician is a professional; to doctor figures is to falsify them, as cooking the books does.

clue.text: Yobs fine with son hanging around island

indicators.note: the fine and son pieces hang around the island letter, surrounding it

parts.note: OK means fine, all right

explanation.surface: Loutish youths, a nice lad among them, loitering about an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Oik is British slang for an uncouth or loutish person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for boorish, ill-mannered young louts; a synonym.

clue.text: Daughter plastered on this?

indicators.note: on is slang for drunk, so the letters of plastered are rearranged, as the setter confirmed

explanation.surface: A daughter got the walls plastered while standing on these steps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastered' looks like the anagram signal (drunk) but is fodder with D; the setter says 'on', also meaning tipsy, does that job. The whole clue doubles as a picture of plastering a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding ladder with flat treads, used by decorators and plasterers to reach walls and ceilings.

clue.text: Perhaps a jolly strippergram (but not all there)

indicators.note: only part of the word strippergram is there, so the answer sits inside it

explanation.surface: A cheeky strip-o-gram act might be fun, though the performer seems a bit dim.
explanation.walkthrough: A jolly is British slang for an outing or junket, so an example of a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: A jolly is British slang for a pleasure outing or jaunt, so an example of an excursion.

clue.text: Drive with idiots out of Top Gear

parts.note: DR is the address abbreviation for drive

indicators.note: the top letter is taken out, so the idiots word loses its first letter

parts.note: mugs are fools or idiots, people easily taken in

explanation.surface: A grumble that the motoring show Top Gear's drivers are idiots who should be dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: Top Gear is a BBC motoring programme; gear is slang for illegal drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear is slang for illicit narcotics, so it stands for the plural noun.

clue.text: Energy-filled blonde with one going concern

indicators.note: the one letter is going, removed from the word
the blonde word is filled with the energy letter, which goes inside it

parts.note: fair-haired means blonde
E is the physics abbreviation for energy
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An energetic blonde and someone leaving: a going concern, a business still trading.
explanation.definitionFit: Fear and concern both mean anxiety or worry about something; a synonym.

clue.text: Parched hill cultivated without nitrogen

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

indicators.note: the cultivated word does without the nitrogen letter

parts.note: refined means cultivated, polished in manners
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A sun-scorched hillside once farmed is now without nitrogen in its soil.
explanation.definitionFit: To torrefy is to dry or roast by heat, so torrefied describes something scorched and parched.

clue.text: Sort of model to cuddle small hooligans

parts.note: the Model T was Henry Ford's early car, so T is a sort of model
a hug is a cuddle
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A kind of fashion model cuddles a few little hooligans.
explanation.definitionFit: Violent ruffians and thugs are the same kind of rough, brawling troublemakers.

clue.text: Nice for one to get stuff in order again

definitions.meaning: Nice in France is an example of a seaside holiday town

definitions.text: to get stuff in order again
definitions.meaning: to sort things a second time

explanation.surface: A trip to Nice to tidy one's things up again.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French Riviera city, not the adjective; the second sense splits as re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice is an example of a holiday town; the second sense reads the word as re-sort, sorting again.

clue.text: Criminal unrest ends in treasonous charges

indicators.note: criminal as in wrong or bent, so the letters of unrest are rearranged
the ends of treasonous are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Criminal unrest leads to charges of treason.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge someone with a task is to entrust it to them; the verb in third person matches.
